blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Biomedical image segmentation must keep up with new anatomical structures, subjects, imaging modalities, and acquisition protocols, yet dense expert annotations are scarce and models trained on one cohort often struggle to transfer. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers a way out: a new structure is specified by a few annotated exemplars at inference time. However, reliable correspondence remains challenging in biomedical images, where adjacent structures often share similar appearances, and variations across subjects and imaging conditions further obscure their distinctions. We introduce CAST, a training-free framework built on a frozen DINOv3 backbone to calibrate fine-grained correspondences. Its stability test improves feature reliability at both global and patch-specific levels, while its coherence test assesses whether candidate correspondences are supported by consistent local structural context. Together, these tests enable more reliable correspondence across diverse anatomical structures and imaging conditions. Across eight biomedical benchmarks spanning 2D and 3D segmentation, cross-subject, and cross-modality transfer, CAST outperforms the strongest overall baseline by 12.34 percentage points in Dice and ranks first across all six volumetric settings. The versatility of CAST further opens up opportunities for challenging biomedical applications, including 2D-to-3D segmentation and atlas label transfer.

difficult to obtain.

blocks.en:
We argue that this matching problem is particularly
challenging in biomedical images.
In many natural-image settings, target objects
exhibit clear appearance differences from
non-target regions.
Biomedical images, however, often contain multiple
adjacent anatomical structures that share tissue
appearance, intensity, and texture, with boundaries
defined by anatomical organization rather than
pronounced visual transitions, as illustrated in Fig. 2 .
The most challenging non-target regions in biomedical
images are often other anatomical structures.
We expect two consequences in frozen feature space.
First, subtle distinctions between neighboring structures
can be obscured by variations induced by geometry,
subject, and acquisition, allowing visually similar
but anatomically incorrect patches to rank above
the correct correspondences.
Second, non-target surroundings are not merely regions
to be rejected, but structured anatomy that provides
additional evidence for distinguishing visually similar
targets.
Consequently, center-level appearance similarity alone
is insufficient for reliable anatomical correspondence.

blocks.en:
If appearance alone cannot be trusted, reliable
correspondences must draw on evidence beyond
individual patch similarity.
Our observation is that annotated exemplars provide
two complementary sources of such evidence:
the stability of visual features under geometric changes
and the spatial organization of labeled anatomy.
We introduce CAST, a training-free framework that
brings these sources together through two tests.
The stability test accounts for feature variations
under geometric transformations, while the coherence
test examines whether candidate matches are consistent
with their surrounding anatomical context.
By combining these complementary cues, CAST establishes
more reliable correspondences between exemplars
and query images, supporting segmentation across
diverse anatomical structures and imaging conditions.
Built upon the transferable representations of a
frozen DINOv3 backbone [ 29 ] ,
CAST requires no additional training or
gradient-based adaptation.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
In-context segmentation. In-context segmentation (ICS) enables new segmentation
tasks to be specified through a few annotated exemplars
at inference time.
Painter [ 34 ] and SegGPT [ 35 ] establish general-purpose visual prompting through
large-scale training, while subsequent methods incorporate
dense feature correspondences into learned segmentation
frameworks [ 22 ] .
Another line leverages pretrained vision foundation
models (VFMs), such as SAM [ 17 ] ,
for visual prompting and exemplar-guided segmentation [ 44 , 19 , 42 ] .
More recently, self-supervised vision transformers [ 2 , 23 , 29 ] have demonstrated strong semantic and spatial properties
in their patch representations, enabling training-free
segmentation through direct feature matching.
INSID3 [ 3 ] combines positional
debiasing with region-level clustering of DINOv3 features,
while FoRIS [ 12 ] progressively refines
foreground correspondences through purification
and consolidation.
FROST [ 26 ] models foreground and
background feature distributions through nonparametric
density estimation.
Other studies explore feature selection, representation
refinement, and background interference [ 41 , 31 , 8 ] .
Despite these advances, reliable patch-level
correspondence remains challenging under geometric
and appearance variations, particularly when feature
similarity alone fails to capture surrounding structure.

blocks.en:
Few-shot biomedical image segmentation. The diversity of anatomical structures and imaging
conditions, together with limited expert annotations,
makes few-shot learning particularly relevant to
biomedical segmentation [ 4 ] .
UniverSeg [ 1 ] and
Tyche [ 27 ] learn to generalize across
segmentation tasks through training on large collections
of annotated medical images.
Subsequent work further explores improved support
selection and similarity-based context refinement,
explicit in-context learning, and broader medical
task coverage [ 5 , 39 , 45 , 38 , 37 , 10 ] .
Medical adaptations of pretrained segmentation models
provide another route to biomedical applications.
MedSAM [ 20 ] extends SAM to medical
images, while MAUP [ 47 ] explores
exemplar-based prompting and HERA [ 21 ] employs test-time adaptation for cross-domain
generalization.
These approaches have also been extended to
volumetric medical imaging [ 6 , 11 , 46 , 7 ] .
Despite these advances, existing approaches often
rely on extensive medical annotations for pretraining,
medical-specific adaptation, or specialized volumetric
representations.
In contrast, we leverage the transferable representations
of a frozen VFM for training-free biomedical
in-context segmentation, without additional
medical-specific pretraining or gradient-based adaptation.

and three MRI → \to CT settings on CHAOS, and
MRI → \to MRI and CT → \to MRI on AMOS22.

are provided in the supplementary material.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We presented CAST, a training-free framework for
biomedical in-context segmentation that makes
frozen visual representations more reliable for
fine-grained anatomical matching.
Across eight biomedical benchmarks covering 2D and 3D
segmentation, cross-subject, and
cross-modality transfer, CAST improves average Dice
by 12.34 percentage points over the strongest baseline
and ranks first across all six volumetric settings.
Beyond conventional benchmarks, CAST achieves
68.48% mean Dice in atlas label transfer, outperforming
the strongest baseline by 6.83 percentage points
when transferring standardized anatomical annotations
to specimen-specific microscopy images.
These results highlight the potential of CAST to
extend reliable segmentation beyond conventional
task-specific settings.
The versatility of CAST opens up broader opportunities
for annotation-efficient biomedical image analysis,
from 2D-to-3D segmentation to atlas-based applications.

68.48% 平均值 地图集标签传输中的骰子, 效果优异
最大基线6.83个百分点
当传输标准化解剖说明时
到标本特定的显微镜图像。
这些结果突出显示了CAST在下列方面的潜力:
